en: So over the last lectures, you learned about
Bun's image API and you also saw that Bun
has a Markdown API. If you didn't go through
those lectures yet, it's now a good time to
do so because in this example here, I'm
combining both. I'm back in a basic website
demo project and of course you find it
attached. And in index.ts, I set up a Bun
server using Bun's serve feature and its
router feature.
And the server we have here has a starting
page, has an articles page and an article
detail page for showing a single article.
And I walk you through the details of what's
happening here in that earlier Markdown
lecture, so I'll not repeat it here.
But if you run the dev server with bun run
dev, you'll open up a server at
localhost:3000.
And if you load that, you'll end up on this
site. And here you can read the articles,
you'll see a list of articles and each
article has an image here that is new
compared to the example from before.
And you also see that image on the article
detail page
along with the rendered Markdown. Now those
images are stored here in the articles
folder next to the article Markdown files
and they were generated with AI again. And
for loading these images, I'm using the Bun
Image API, that's new in this example here.
So what you'll see in this index.ts file is
that we got all the server-related code, we
got code for finding the article files, the
Markdown files here,
and for then extracting the front matter,
the metadata at top of the Markdown files,
so this part here, and then also the raw
Markdown content below.
In that front matter, you also find
thumbnail data, so the name of the image
file and some alt text. And in index.ts,
we're then loading and transforming those
images with help of Bun's image API. And
that is happening here in this render
thumbnail function. renderThumbnail, in case
you're wondering, is called for this route,
which was also added, which is the route for
loading an image. So they are generated on
the fly. And if your website would then be
hosted behind some cache, behind Cloudflare,
for example, those images would of course be
cached and not be regenerated for every
request. So that we have a route that will
trigger the image generation. Now, what do I
mean with generation?
I mean the transformation and optimization
of these images, the generation of some new
improved images therefore.
Now, first we check whether a valid image
file path is requested, then we try loading
that input file and we return a NotFound
error if we don't find it. But then
thereafter, we're using the Bun Image API,
so the image method here
on the loaded file, that is what we're doing
here,
we're using it to resize the image
and target these predefined thumbnail width
and height settings so that even if the
original images were much bigger, we get
those smaller images and we don't load all
that unnecessary data for every request.
And I then also ensure that we always render
out WebP files, which is an image format
optimized for web
so that no matter if it's a JPEG or PNG or
whatever input image, we return a WebP file.
And I then get the raw blob here instead of
writing it to a file. So in the past
lecture, we used write to store the
optimized image somewhere. Here I'm getting
the blob instead because that blob is in the
end what I wanna return in my response. The
optimized thumbnail is that blob which I'm
returning because that is a valid response
value when using the standard response API
which Bun is using.
And I even have my own basic cache setting
here where I cache the file by filename, but
we could disable that in development if we
would want to turn it off or if we were
hosting this page behind a real
cache provider like Cloudflare, as mentioned
before.
I also have the getThumbnailPlaceholder
function here,
which is called when rendering an article
page so that we do indeed show a placeholder
right away whilst we're waiting for the
original image to load. Though if you're
running this development server locally on
your machine, the image will load so quickly
that you probably won't see the placeholder.
But the placeholder is created with the
placeholder API provided by Bun and then
embedded into those returned responses, into
those returned HTML pages in that thumb
via that thumbnail placeholder property
here.
So if you take a look at the templates, at
article.html for example,
you see that in there I have this
placeholder as a background image. And that
in the end is then overwritten once that
image loaded in, once the real image is
available. But we use this approach to have
a nice placeholder whilst we're waiting for
the raw image to be loaded.
And that is therefore how you could use the
Bun Image API in a
real example on a real webpage so that
again, you could build a basic personal
website like this, a personal blog like this
without any other dependencies Nothing else,
nothing other than Bun, just Bun's Markdown
rendering and its image optimization
feature.
